subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: building in rest and respite for the caregiver [Thinking]
passage: Sit down, beta. I am Alka, and I will tell you something I learned at twenty-six, when I was looking after my mother and holding down a job. For months I ran on nothing. One evening I fell asleep at the dining table with the spoon in my hand and thought: if I break, who does the caring? It is not a sprint. It is more like a long journey, and you must plan where you will rest. So I told my brother Francis, "Every Thursday evening is mine. Please be here from six." He did not argue. On Thursdays I walked, or sat with a friend, or did nothing at all. Amma was well looked after, and I had energy again the next day. That one evening off is what kept the rest going.

qa.q: Which evening did Alka ask Francis to cover?
What was Alka feeling on the evening she fell asleep at the table?
qa.a: Alka felt alarm and fear of breaking down, shown by wondering who would do the caring if that happened.

qa.q: What choice did Alka make that changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Alka asked Francis to cover Thursday evenings so that rest was built in, and the regular rest brought back the energy to keep caring.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt when Alka asked?
qa.a: Francis may have felt glad to be given a clear, doable role, since he did not argue.

grounding: Alka recalls scheduling a weekly evening off, covered by Francis, as part of planning care for the long run.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: building in rest and respite for the caregiver [Thinking]
passage:
It was audit month at the bank where Yamini worked, and her mother's dialysis days hadn't moved: Monday, Wednesday, Friday. For three weeks Yamini had gone from office to hospital to home to laptop, sleeping five hours a night.
On Thursday her friend Damini found her crying in the office washroom.
"You can't do this for years like this," Damini said.
That night, Yamini thought it through. Amma's care wasn't ending next month. It would go on for a long time. If she collapsed, who would take Amma to the hospital? Her own energy wasn't a luxury; it was part of the plan.
She called her brother Arvind. "I need one evening a week off. Fixed. Every Friday, you do the hospital and dinner with Amma."
He was quiet, then said, "I should have offered long ago."
The next Friday, Yamini went to a movie with Damini. She didn't check her phone once.

qa.q: On which days did Yamini's mother have dialysis?
How did Yamini feel when Damini found her in the washroom?
qa.a: Yamini was exhausted and overwhelmed, crying after weeks of little sleep and constant rushing.

qa.q: What else could Yamini add to make the care sustainable?
qa.a: Yamini could ask about a second fixed break or some paid help, and review the plan with Arvind every few months.

qa.q: How might Arvind see Yamini's request?
qa.a: Arvind seems a little guilty but willing, admitting he should have offered long ago and taking Fridays.

grounding: It shows a caregiver realising her own energy matters, scheduling a weekly evening off and asking her brother to cover it, planning care as a long journey.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: building in rest and respite for the caregiver [Thinking]
passage:
Usha had looked after her father in their Ahmedabad flat for eight months since his Parkinson's got worse. Mornings before work, evenings after, and every weekend.
One Sunday she forgot to switch off the gas under the milk and only noticed when the smell filled the kitchen. She sat down on the floor, shaking.
"This isn't a sprint," she thought. "Papa might need me for years. If I burn out, he loses his carer."
That evening she called her brother Nilesh, who lived across the city. "I need one evening off a week. Every Wednesday. You come, give Papa dinner, sit with him. I'll go out, or just sleep."
Nilesh hesitated. "Wednesdays are difficult."
"Then pick a day. But one day, every week."
"Thursday," he said finally.
The first Thursday, Usha went to her old dance class. She came home humming, and her father noticed.

qa.q: Which day did Nilesh finally agree to?
How did Usha feel sitting on the kitchen floor?
qa.a: Usha felt frightened and shaken after forgetting the gas, realising how worn out she had become.

qa.q: What else could Usha do to protect her energy?
qa.a: She could add another small break, such as a weekend morning, or look into part-time help for her father.

qa.q: How might Usha's father see the change?
qa.a: Her father notices her coming home humming, so he may feel relieved and less guilty that she has some life of her own.

grounding: It shows a caregiver recognising her own energy matters, scheduling a weekly evening off and asking her brother to cover it, planning care for the long run.
